title: What is going on in education in England?
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Daisy Christodoulou reviews the 2025 PISA results for an international readership and argues that England has resisted a global decline in reading and maths scores. She points to the natural experiment inside the UK, where England's knowledge-based curriculum, terminal exams, phonics and teacher-led classrooms have been followed by steady scores while the more progressive systems in Scotland and Wales have fallen sharply. She answers the objection that PISA may be unreliable by noting that PISA is itself a progressive, problem-solving test that should favour Scotland and Wales, and that England also does well on TIMSS and PIRLS. Drawing on E.D. Hirsch's analogy with medicine, she argues that the test-score statistics and the cognitive science of working memory and prior knowledge now point the same way. She then sketches cheap next steps, such as training 100 leaders to turn around 100 struggling schools and spreading best practice, and closes by noting the irony that the new government wants to move away from the policies other countries now want to study.
points: England's relative PISA success is presented as a natural experiment, since England, Scotland and Wales diverged after 2010 and only the knowledge-focused system held its scores.

Christodoulou argues the strongest reply to the 'can we trust PISA' question is that PISA is a progressive, skills-style test and England still outperforms on it, with TIMSS and PIRLS giving the same result.
Following Hirsch, she says two kinds of evidence are needed, outcome statistics and cognitive science, and that for England both now agree.

Her practical proposal is to spread existing best practice, for example by training a cadre of 100 leaders from successful schools to lead 100 struggling ones, rather than wait for a scientific breakthrough.
She flags a policy paradox: other countries are asking to learn from England just as its government plans to reverse the reforms.
quotes: The big global headline was that the OECD average scores on maths and reading were the lowest ever recorded in the history of the tests. And a very significant sub-plot is that England is one of the very few countries to have resisted this downward trend.

But whilst England’s scores have held steady, Scotland and Wales have declined sharply. 15-year-olds in England used to be behind those in Scotland. They are now about a year ahead in maths and science, and ahead by a smaller amount in reading.

In short, PISA is a screen-based test of problem-solving skills that requires limited specific curriculum knowledge. If you wanted to design a test that would be least likely to reward England’s educational approach, and most likely to reward the approach in Scotland & Wales, it would be PISA.

We are now in the situation where the statistics and the underlying science are pointing in the same direction. England adopted an approach to education explicitly influenced by Hirsch and insights from cognitive science. It is now outperforming many countries on international educational surveys.

And to improve education, we could gain a lot just by doing better at spreading existing best practice. That is to say, even without any big new scientific breakthroughs, we could still improve just by making effective teaching methods more widely used.
The whole world is worrying about their kids getting dumber. England appear to have the policy solution. And yet the government in England seem to want to reverse those policies.
